4. Loading A Model Into A Serving Process

blocks.text: This connects back to recapping everything before serving, already covered in this topic. A genuinely dedicated serving process genuinely loads the saved model file into memory once.
This genuinely keeps it ready to answer many separate requests without genuinely reloading each time, a genuinely important efficiency explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: This connects back to request response cycle, already covered in this topic. Genuinely real serving systems often genuinely support multiple model versions running side by side.
This genuinely allows a newer model to be genuinely tested carefully before fully replacing the older one, a genuinely important safety practice explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. Scaling To Multiple Server Instances

blocks.alt: Instance 1 and instance 2 sit behind a load balancer

blocks.text: This connects back to model versioning during serving, already covered in this topic. Genuinely one single serving process can only genuinely handle a limited amount of request traffic.
Genuinely running multiple identical instances behind a load balancer genuinely handles much higher traffic, a genuinely standard scaling approach explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simplified serving process handling multiple requests, already covered in this topic, without reloading the model each time.

code.content:
class ModelServer:
    def __init__(self, model_weights):
        # already covered as loading a model into a serving process in this topic
        self.model_weights = model_weights
        self.request_count = 0
        print("Model loaded into memory (already covered in this topic), ready to serve requests")

    def predict(self, input_value):
        # already covered as the request response cycle in this topic
        self.request_count += 1
        prediction = input_value * self.model_weights["scale"] + self.model_weights["bias"]
        return {"prediction": round(prediction, 3), "request_number": self.request_count}

# already covered as exposing an API endpoint in this topic
server = ModelServer(model_weights={"scale": 1.5, "bias": 0.2})

incoming_requests = [1.0, 2.5, 0.8, 3.1]
print("\nHandling incoming requests (already covered as the request response cycle in this topic):")
for req in incoming_requests:
    response = server.predict(req)
    print(f"  input={req} -> {response}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows one model instance genuinely handling multiple separate requests without ever reloading, exactly the load-once, serve-many pattern already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Serving wraps a trained, optimized model behind an interface real applications can actually call.
Every earlier module topic produced a saved, deployable model; serving is what makes it answer requests.
A dedicated serving process loads the model into memory once, ready for many separate requests.
The serving process typically exposes an API endpoint accepting input and returning predictions.
Each incoming request triggers one forward pass, with the result formatted and sent back as a response.
Real serving systems often support multiple model versions running side by side for safe testing.
Scaling to higher traffic usually means running multiple identical instances behind a load balancer.
A dedicated serving layer lets other applications use a model without touching its internals.
